title: Scope, goals and client-defined success
audience: Coordinators, support workers and trained cleaners who may be asked to work in a home affected by hoarding or environmental neglect, as part of an authorised support plan. Not a qualification or authority to clear a property, dispose of a resident's belongings, enter by force, or provide welfare or clinical support.
learningOutcomes: Define the scope of work from the objective the resident has approved.
Distinguish a safety improvement from a full-property clearance and state which one is being done.
Record the permitted areas and the decisions that need fresh permission before any item is moved.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson is training content. It does not authorise entry to a home by force, clearance of belongings, handling of hazardous material, or welfare or clinical assessment. Completing it gives no licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the law that applies where the work takes place.

instruction.heading: Start from the resident's objective
instruction.body: Every job in this area starts with an objective the resident has approved. The objective may be narrow, such as keeping the route to the bathroom and the front door clear, or broader. A safety improvement reduces a specific named risk, such as a blocked exit or combustible material near a heater. A full-property clearance removes most of the contents. It is a different decision that needs its own consent, handling, waste and support arrangements. Workers drift from one to the other when a deadline or a property manager's demand replaces the resident's own words. Keep the two apart on paper. Fire Rescue Victoria recommends that risk reduction be a priority rather than large scale removal, which is a sound reason to keep the aim narrow and to agree it with the resident first.

instruction.heading: Recording the scope and what is unverified
instruction.body: Write a short scope record: the objective in the resident's words, the areas for work, the actions allowed, the items that need a fresh decision, and the people who may decide. Note what you have seen yourself, what others have told you, and what is still unverified. Any change needs supervisor clearance and a note of who asked for it. Permission is never inferred from a key, a deadline or a family member's view. Where the resident has not clearly agreed to a change, the work stays within the existing record, and the request is referred.

procedure: Stop. Do not move any item until the objective and the consent for the area are recorded.
Ask the resident to state, in their own words, the safety goal they want achieved.
Write the scope record: objective, permitted areas, permitted actions, items needing fresh decisions, and the decision makers.
List separately what you have seen directly, what was reported by others, and what remains unverified.
Compare any other request, including from a manager or a relative, against the scope record. Do not act on requests outside it.
Obtain supervisor clearance before any change to the scope, and file the change with its date.

workedExamples.situation: A property manager demands removal of all contents, but the resident has approved only clearing the route to the bathroom.
workedExamples.reasoning: The approved boundary is the route the resident chose. The manager's demand is not a resident decision. Document the limited safety goal, record the disagreement, and refer the authority dispute before any item is moved.

workedExamples.situation: The resident wants the bathroom and hallway usable again. The support worker thinks the whole living room should also be cleared.
workedExamples.reasoning: The scope is the bathroom and hallway the resident has chosen. The living-room clearance is a different objective that needs its own consent. Leave the living room as it is, record the difference and raise it with the coordinator for a fresh decision.

equipmentAndPpe: Scope record template with the objective, permitted areas, permitted actions and the decision makers.
Simple notebook or tablet record for observed, reported and unverified information, with dates.
Training-only role-play cards. No real belongings, stacks or waste are handled in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Treating a deadline or a manager's instruction as the resident's objective.
commonErrors.prevention: Work from the resident-approved scope record. Refer any broader demand.

commonErrors.error: Using a safety goal as cover for a full clearance.
commonErrors.prevention: Name the objective in the scope record and stop when the approved objective is met.

commonErrors.error: Recording only the outcome that was wanted, not what was seen or is unverified.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep observed, reported and unverified information in separate, dated entries.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant authority to clear or dispose of belongings. Completing it gives no licence, certificate or approval.

Fire Rescue Victoria's hoarding guidance is Victorian. It is not a legal determination for other states or territories, and the rules that apply where the work takes place must be checked with the coordinator.

qualityStandard: The learner states the resident-approved objective in one sentence and separates it from a full clearance.
The learner records the permitted areas, actions and the decisions that need fresh permission.
The learner stops and refers any request that goes beyond the scope record.
documentationEvidence: Scope record with the objective, permitted areas and actions, and the decision makers.
Observed, reported and unverified information listed separately, with dates.
Supervisor clearance for any change to the scope.
summary: The resident's approved objective defines the work.
A safety improvement is not a full clearance.
Record the scope, the decision makers and what is unverified before anything moves.
A broader demand is referred, not accepted.

knowledgeChecks.question: A property manager asks for all contents to be removed. The resident has approved clearing only the route to the bathroom. What is the approved scope?
options: All contents, because the manager is the client.
The route to the bathroom that the resident approved, with the manager's request recorded and referred.
Whatever can be moved in one day.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement best separates a safety improvement from a full-property clearance?
options: They are the same job, done at different speeds.
A safety improvement is any job that takes less than a day.
A safety improvement reduces a specific named risk, while a full clearance removes most contents and needs its own consent.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is a valid reason to change the agreed scope?
options: The resident has clearly agreed to the change and a supervisor has cleared it in writing.
The deadline is close and the crew has spare time.
A relative holding a key asked for more to be removed.

The page says FRV firefighters respond to a fire or emergency where there is hoarding or environmental neglect every 4 to 6 days; hoarding increases the risk of having a fire; accumulated possessions result in an abnormally high fuel load; and FRV recommends risk reduction as a priority rather than large scale removal. Publisher: Fire Rescue Victoria.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a home by force, to clear, sort or dispose of a resident's belongings without valid consent, to handle or dispose of hazardous waste, to deal with unstable stacks or structural hazards, or to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the local law. Tenancy, safeguarding and information-sharing rights are jurisdiction-specific, and fire-risk, structural, pest and hazardous-waste decisions belong to the competent authorities and specialists named in the plan. Where authority or consent is unclear, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: consent is not specific, documented and current; the resident has objected or withdrawn consent; a party seeks entry by force, nonconsensual disposal or removal of personal documents; a fire-load, ignition, egress or obstruction hazard is present; a stack or structure is unstable; pests, unknown liquids or mouldy goods are present; sharps, chemicals or unknown containers are found; waste would go to general disposal without characterisation; private information is requested without authority; or the work would go beyond the approved plan. Stopping is a valid professional outcome. Record the disagreement, protect the resident's choices and refer the authority dispute before any property is moved.
